analysis.one_liner: Lets people wipe out private student loan debt in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its subcommittee from May 2011 until the Congress ended in January 2013, with 46 Democratic cosponsors but no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2005, private student loans—those issued by banks and other lenders, not the government—can almost never be erased in bankruptcy unless the borrower proves 'undue hardship,' a standard most people cannot meet. This bill would change the law so only government-backed or nonprofit-funded loans keep that special protection, letting borrowers discharge private student loan debt just like credit card or medical debt. It never received a hearing, a vote, or any action after being sent to the House Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers drowning in private student loan debt who file for bankruptcy. Today they must sue their own lenders inside bankruptcy court and prove that repaying would cause 'undue hardship'—a vague test that is expensive to litigate and that most filers fail. The bill would let them erase these loans through the normal bankruptcy process, giving a fresh start to people who took out high-interest private loans, often to cover costs that federal aid did not.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the pre-2005 rule under which private student loans could be discharged in bankruptcy without proving undue hardship [S2][S3].
Keeps the special protection only for loans made, insured, or guaranteed by a government, or funded by a government program or by a nonprofit [S2][S3].
Applies to bankruptcy cases filed after the bill's enactment, so borrowers already in bankruptcy would not be affected retroactively [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private student lenders, who would no longer hold nearly unbreakable claims and would face more losses when borrowers go bankrupt. Lenders argue they would respond by charging higher interest rates or lending less, since bankruptcy risk would return as a cost of doing business.

drawbacks.text: Lenders could raise rates or tighten credit: making private loans dischargeable adds bankruptcy risk that lenders typically price into their loans, which could mean higher costs for future student borrowers.
Bankruptcy filings specifically to shed student debt could increase, since the 'undue hardship' barrier would no longer stop borrowers from including private loans in a routine discharge.
The relief reaches only people who file for bankruptcy—a narrow, desperate group—so it does nothing for the far larger population of borrowers who are struggling but not in bankruptcy court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it restores ordinary bankruptcy protections to a group of borrowers in the most severe financial distress, at a cost borne by private lenders and potentially spread as slightly higher rates to future borrowers. Critics' strongest point—that easier discharge could raise private loan rates—has to be weighed against the fact that these loans already carry relatively high rates and that the pre-2005 rule coexisted with a functioning private lending market. The bill is a targeted fix, not a solution to overall student debt.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and stayed there—no hearing, no vote, nothing—until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on May 26, 2011, with 16 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced [S1][S5].
On July 11, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts, Commercial and Administrative Law—the last recorded action of the bill [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or a Senate companion vote during the 112th Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders keep their nearly unbreakable claims on borrowers, since the law still treats private student loans as virtually impossible to erase in bankruptcy.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 46 cosponsors [S1][S4].

for.name: 46 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; support was entirely from one party [S4].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over bankruptcy law
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill went to a subcommittee in July 2011 and no further action was ever recorded [S5].

against.name: Private student loan industry
against.role: Lenders holding nondischargeable student debt (e.g., Sallie Mae, banks, loan servicers)
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the 2005 law the bill would repeal and had a direct financial stake in its defeat; industry lobbying against dischargeability changes was widely reported.

sides.party_line_note: All 46 cosponsors were Democrats and none of the 17 original sponsors was a Republican; the Republican-controlled House committee never acted on it [S1][S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill strips private student loans of their special status as debts that survive bankruptcy, exposing lenders to losses when borrowers file. Lenders' interest in keeping the 2005 rule runs directly against distressed borrowers who need a discharge.

industries.industry: Federal government and nonprofit loan programs
industries.note: The bill keeps the 'undue hardship' protection for government-backed and nonprofit-funded loans, preserving the federal student loan system's privileged claim status even as private competitors lose it.
